chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
title: Singin' the Blues, Trumbauer and Red Nichols
summary: Trumbauer's Singin' the Blues solo was pretty and original; he also liked Red Nichols's bands, a different jazz from Fletcher Henderson's.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: You told me at one point that one of the bands you were in had an arrangement of "Singin' The Blues" that Trumbauer did.
That was something that was extremely popular. I guess that record really made it. Why did it have such a strong

Well, it was a pretty solo and it was a very original type of thing. The thing went...[SINGS REFRAIN]... You see, the way he put his originality into it and made it... They could have made a song out of that. Do you know what I mean?
They could have made a song out of what he played.
And I guess also it wasn't usual for someone to take a whole chorus on a record.
No, the record was all right. It was great! Yeah, that band was great anyhow. I liked Frankie Trumbauer. I had seen Red Nichols' bands. I used to like them.
Yeah, they had a different type of Jazz than Fletcher Henderson, you know. They had a different type, but it was great. You know? And the piano player played block chords, you know...
So those things... There wasn't any real tendency to look at...because those were White musicians, to look at
that as a different kind of music.
